Cases Deaths Hospitalizations Vaccines Variants Wastewater Data About More resources More COVID-19 Cases, %%COUNTRY%% WHO will utilize various sources to continue monitoring the COVID-19 epidemiological situation via the WHO COVID-19 dashboard. If data for certain countries is unavailable in this section, it may indicate that they have either ceased reporting COVID-19 surveillance data to WHO or have integrated the COVID-19 surveillance into existing respiratory disease surveillance. In the latter case, SARS-CoV-2 detections from sentinel and systematic virological surveillance sites in those countries may be found in the Circulation section which also includes information on SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation. This global summary of COVID-19 cases includes data on confirmed cases reported to WHO from the comprehensive COVID-19 case monitoring. Coronavirus (COVID-19) cases, %%COUNTRY%% data Source: World Health Organization Loading... Loading... Loading... What is the definition of 'confirmed' and 'reported' in COVID-19 data? All data represents the date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. In the context of WHO's statistical reporting of COVID-19 data, it is important to note that only confirmed cases are included in case and death counts. In guidance updated on 22 July 2023; there are two alternative definitions for 'Confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection' in international surveillance reporting, although some departures may exist due to local adaptations: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria OR epidemiological criteria. b) A person meeting clinical criteria AND/OR epidemiological criteria (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. Additionally, WHO only disseminates data as reported by its Member States. From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data has been compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported directly to WHO headquarters by Member States. Statistical counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these statistics at a global level. Please note that statistics do not necessarily reflect the actual number of cases and deaths or the actual number of countries where cases and deaths are occurring, as a number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting. Trends in COVID-19 cases, %%COUNTRY%% Recent COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, July 2023 - present Source: World Health Organization Data may be incomplete for the latest week. Total COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, January 2020 - present Source: World Health Organization Why is COVID-19 data being presented as weekly statistics? A number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting COVID-19 case and death counts to WHO. An outcome of these differences in reporting is that WHO may receive daily data from some countries, while other countries may only report data to WHO once every 14 days. In addition, countries differ in how they choose to report statistics; some countries provide their data attributed to specific dates while others who report less frequently may group data from 7 days into a single statistic attributed to a week in their reporting. As of 25 August 2023, WHO declared that it is no longer necessary for Member States to report daily counts of cases and deaths to WHO and requested strengthening of weekly reporting. Reported data is still available attributed to specific dates (daily data) here as a download. This dashboard presents the same statistics as weekly figures in charts in order to mitigate against the visual misinterpretation of data. Should daily data have been presented here, many countries would show zero counts for multiple consecutive days due in part to the differences in how they choose to report. While weekly intervals do not completely mitigate against this, the approach reduces the risk that some dashboard users might infer zero cases or deaths when lack of data is often due to reporting differences. What do negative counts of cases or deaths mean? All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected by Member States at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections in their reporting. Bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. Aggregate groups (weekly data to week end date) Source: World Health Organization COVID-19 cases, country level trends Percent change based on previous 28 days Source: World Health Organization Metadata Glossary and definitions Confirmed COVID-19 case Although COVID-19 defines the symptomatic disease caused by SARS-CoV-2, the cases are presented in this dashboard meet one of two alternate definitions of confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection in international surveillance reporting: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria* OR epidemiological criteria*. b) A person meeting clinical criteria* AND/OR epidemiological criteria* (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. *Please visit the WHO COVID-19 Case definition for details on clinical and epidemiological criteria. Updated 22 July 2023 Last 7 days ‘Last 7 days’ refers to the most recent complete epidemiological week (commonly referred to as an 'epi week'). Last 28 days ‘Last 28 days’ refers to the four preceding most recently complete epidemiological weeks. WHO Regions The World Health Organization (WHO) is divided into six regions with regional offices, each responsible for addressing health challenges and promoting public health within its designated geographical area. These regions serve as administrative units that allow the WHO to tailor its efforts to the specific needs, priorities, and health conditions of member countries within each region. World Bank Income Groups The World Bank classifies economies into income groups based on their Gross National Income (GNI) per capita. These annually updated classifications help the World Bank and other organizations analyze and understand global economic trends, allocate resources, and design development policies. Data sources COVID-19 case data From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data is compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported to WHO headquarters. WHO COVID-19 Dashboard is updated every Tuesday for the period of two full weeks prior. Counts primarily reflect laboratory-confirmed cases and deaths, based upon WHO case definitions; although some departures may exist due to local adaptations. Counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these data at a global level. All data represent date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data are subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals. New case and death counts from the Region of the Americas Starting from the week commencing on 11 September 2023, the source of the data from the Region of the Americas was switched to the aggregated national surveillances, received through the COVID-19, Influenza, RSV and Other Respiratory Viruses program in the Americas. Data have been included retrospectively since 31 July 2023. Rates <0.001 per 100,000 population may be rounded to 0. Conducted by an interdisciplinary team of researchers from Aga Khan University in Karachi and published in the Brazilian Journal of Microbiology, the study evaluated the post-pandemic diversification of viral lineages following the formal conclusion of the global public health emergency. While high-income Western countries experienced rapid lineage turnovers where JN.1 was swiftly displaced by newer sub-lineages such as KP.3.1.1 by mid-2024, circulating viral populations in Pakistan demonstrated an extended duration of JN.1 dominance that lasted through the third quarter of 2024. This sustained prevalence occurred alongside substantial genomic entropy, offering valuable empirical insights into how regional transmission patterns, diagnostic infrastructure, and baseline population exposures modulate SARS-CoV-2 molecular evolution across diverse geographic environments. The central research objective focused on addressing substantial knowledge gaps concerning post-2023 SARS-CoV-2 molecular epidemiology within South Asia, where systematic genomic surveillance has historically been constrained relative to high-throughput surveillance programs in North America and Western Europe. To investigate how circulating lineages in Pakistan compared against international benchmarks, the investigators accessed public sequence repositories alongside clinical diagnostic specimens to analyze phylogenetic diversity, nucleotide substitution rates, and positional entropy across the viral genome. By establishing a rigorous comparative framework that contrasted Pakistani viral sequences against standardized cohorts from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and neighboring India, the researchers sought to determine whether post-pandemic viral populations followed a synchronized global trajectory or diverged in response to local epidemiological conditions. The resulting analyses demonstrate that while basic evolutionary mechanisms and substitution kinetics remain broadly comparable across continents, the actual composition and temporal persistence of dominant clades can vary markedly across jurisdictions. Discover more Tour Colleges Study Biology Study Chemistry To construct their primary observational dataset, the investigators retrieved genomic records deposited in the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data EpiCoV database between January 2023 and September 2024, filtering for complete genomes that exhibited more than 95 percent sequence coverage, fewer than 1 percent ambiguous nucleotide calls, and verified collection dates and regional metadata. From an initial national download of 976 SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Pakistan, the researchers excluded travel-associated cases and duplicate entries, ultimately grouping 41 low-frequency lineages according to their designated Nextstrain clades while preserving overarching phylogenetic relationships to yield a focused dataset of 935 representative genomes for temporal analysis. Temporal coverage within this national repository varied across the surveillance timeframe, with sequencing frequency reaching its highest peak in March 2023 with 343 analyzed genomes, followed by a secondary peak of 109 genomes in March 2024, reflecting operational realities where routine molecular testing ebbed and flowed alongside fluctuating clinical demand. Discover more Engineering Job Board Research Paper Access Learn Engineering Track Biotech Complementing the national GISAID sequence repository, the research team conducted an in-depth retrospective laboratory evaluation of 282 nasopharyngeal swab specimens confirmed positive for SARS-CoV-2 via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assays at the Aga Khan University Hospital Clinical Laboratories. Because the hospital operates a diagnostic network comprising more than 300 sample collection centers distributed throughout Pakistan, the laboratory cohort provided access to standardized clinical testing data and patient demographics that are frequently absent from international public sequence databases. Diagnostic screening was performed using the automated Roche Cobas 6800 system targeting the Orf1ab genetic region, and positive samples demonstrating cycle threshold values of 35 or lower were systematically charted to observe local testing trends. Of these confirmed diagnostic specimens, a subset of 223 samples satisfied the stringent quality criteria established for whole genome sequencing, which required a cycle threshold value of 26 or below to ensure sufficient template density for high-throughput multiplex library construction. The methodological workflow for clinical sequencing involved reverse transcribing viral ribonucleic acid into complementary DNA using specialized commercial synthesis kits, followed by dual-pool multiplex PCR amplification using validated ARTIC network version 3 primers designed specifically for SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery. Amplicons were converted into sequencing libraries using Illumina Nextera DNA Flex protocols and subsequently resolved on an Illumina MiSeq sequencing platform. Bioinformatic processing was carried out via the cloud-based CZID computational platform, which filtered out human host reads using minimap2 alignments against the human reference genome before aligning residual reads against the ancestral Wuhan-Hu-1 reference sequence NC_045512.2. Adaptor sequences were removed using Trim Galore, base calls were strictly retained only when sequence depth exceeded 10-fold coverage, and consensus variants were identified using samtools and BCFtools v1.20 to ensure analytical fidelity prior to downstream phylogenetic reconstruction. Phylogenetic lineage designations for the assembled genomes were systematically assigned using the Pangolin tool with the pangoLEARN algorithmic model, while Nextstrain clade classifications and amino acid substitutions were verified through Nextclade version 3.5.0. Multiple sequence alignments of complete viral genomes were generated using MAFFT version 7.505, after which maximum-likelihood phylogenetic trees were constructed utilizing IQ-TREE version 2.2.0 parameterized under the general time-reversible model with gamma-distributed rate heterogeneity across sites. Evolutionary rates and branch lengths were computed using the Augur bioinformatics pipeline and TreeTime within a time-resolved framework, where molecular clock outliers were filtered using a four-times interquartile range threshold. To assess site-specific amino acid variability, positional Shannon entropy across all ten open reading frames was calculated mathematically based on the relative frequencies of observed residues, with visual representations generated in Auspice, FigTree, and custom R scripts. For international comparisons, the authors assembled global datasets from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and India over the identical twenty-one-month surveillance window. Because raw submission counts in GISAID were heavily skewed—ranging from 286,135 sequences from the United States to 14,734 sequences from India—the authors executed a monthly down-sampling algorithm to standardize statistical comparisons. Specifically, custom Python routines selected up to 300 representative genomes per country-month, retaining all available sequences whenever monthly submissions fell below that threshold. This normalization strategy generated standardized comparison datasets consisting of 6,300 genomes each for the United States, the United Kingdom, and France, alongside 3,435 genomes for India. Combining these standardized international cohorts with 780 representative Pakistani genomes enabled the construction of a comprehensive, time-resolved maximum-likelihood tree spanning Nextstrain clades 21L through 24E, providing an empirical basis for comparing lineage turnover and evolutionary rates across disparate health systems. Analysis of national lineage dynamics in Pakistan revealed a clear temporal progression among 86 distinct identified variants, though only 13 achieved relative monthly frequencies exceeding 20 percent. During the first half of 2023, viral populations were heavily dominated by recombinant XBB lineages, particularly XBB.1.19.1 and XBB.1.9.1, which collectively accounted for 39 percent of characterized genomes in March 2023. By August 2023, these ancestral recombinants were replaced by emerging sub-lineages GW.5, GW.5.1, and persistent XBB.1.19.1 strains, before transitioning toward FL.1 and FY.5 by October 2023. The pivotal evolutionary transition occurred in late 2023 with the introduction of the BA.2.86-descended variant JN.1. Unlike Western comparison countries, where JN.1 was rapidly superseded by newer progeny such as KP.3.1.1 during the spring and summer of 2024, Pakistan experienced prolonged JN.1 dominance throughout the surveillance window, with JN.1 and its sub-lineage JN.1.18 representing 77 percent of sequenced isolates in March 2024 and remaining predominant through September 2024 despite sporadic detections of KP.2, LB.1, and LA.1. Demographic and epidemiological evaluations performed on 213 sequenced samples at the Aga Khan University Hospital revealed that the vast majority of analyzed specimens originated from Sindh province, with Karachi and Hyderabad accounting for 94.8 percent of cases, alongside sporadic submissions from Punjab, Islamabad Capital Territory, Gilgit-Baltistan, Baluchistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Patient age distributions indicated that adults aged 19 to 50 years comprised 54 percent of positive cases, older adults aged over 50 years represented 44 percent, and pediatric individuals aged 1 to 18 years accounted for 3 percent. Statistical evaluations revealed no significant linear trend in case numbers across the study period via chi-square testing, reflecting intermittent wave-like epidemic surges rather than continuous increases. Furthermore, categorical analysis of 21 lineages across patient characteristics demonstrated no statistically significant associations between specific SARS-CoV-2 lineages and patient gender via Fisher’s exact test, patient age categories via chi-square analysis, or inpatient versus outpatient clinical status. When assessing molecular clock kinetics, the estimated nucleotide substitution rate for SARS-CoV-2 in Pakistan was calculated at 4.67 times 10 to the negative fourth power substitutions per site per year, accompanied by a 95 percent confidence interval extending from 3.29 times 10 to the negative fourth power to 6.04 times 10 to the negative fourth power. This measured substitution rate was statistically indistinguishable from the rates calculated for Western nations, where point estimates ranged between 4.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power and 5.22 times 10 to the negative fourth power per site per year. Formal meta-analytic evaluation using Cochran’s Q test confirmed an absence of significant overall heterogeneity among substitution rates observed in Pakistan, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. In contrast, genomes analyzed from India exhibited a significantly lower estimated substitution rate of 6.92 times 10 to the negative fifth power per site per year, though this figure was accompanied by an unusually wide confidence interval ranging from zero to 1.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power, suggesting underlying data constraints or differences in lineage sampling rather than true biological divergence. Genomic diversity analyses revealed that SARS-CoV-2 isolates in Pakistan exhibited a mean positional Shannon entropy of 0.0324 across the complete coding sequence, a figure noticeably higher than the baseline positional entropy values recorded for the United States at 0.0100, the United Kingdom at 0.0107, France at 0.0105, and India at 0.0129. Across all examined geographical regions, mutational density was consistently concentrated within the spike glycoprotein gene region, followed by open reading frame 1ab and the membrane protein gene, aligning with known selective pressures directed against viral surface antigens. While the elevated genomic entropy observed in Pakistan mirrors findings from prolonged national surveillance in other settings where post-outbreak diversification accumulates, the study authors explicitly noted that this elevated metric could partially reflect sampling dynamics inherent to smaller, geographically concentrated datasets rather than purely elevated viral mutation rates in vivo. Interpretation of these epidemiological findings must be framed within several methodological and structural limitations acknowledged by the investigators. First, the total volume of genomic sequencing performed in Pakistan was modest compared to high-resource nations, driven by constrained diagnostic resources where national testing capacity peaked at approximately 46,500 tests daily during 2021 compared to 1 million daily tests in the United States. Second, because clinical severity metrics and vaccination histories were unavailable for the vast majority of sequenced isolates, the authors could not directly correlate specific lineage replacements with clinical outcomes or immune breakthrough frequencies. Third, geographic representation was heavily skewed toward Sindh province due to the centralized location of the sequencing infrastructure in Karachi, leaving rural provinces underrepresented. Despite these constraints, the study provides foundational documentation of post-pandemic viral evolution in Pakistan, illustrating how regional vaccine platforms—dominated by inactivated formulations such as Sinopharm and SinoVac—alongside distinct population demographics can foster localized evolutionary niches that sustain major viral lineages long after their global displacement. records.content_title: Current booster vaccine protects against new PJ.2.1 SARS-CoV-2 variant
records.content: Germany's COVID-19 traffic light is on red ( https://corona-ampel.de/ ), and the number of infections is high. But how well is the population protected against the virus variants currently circulating? The new SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 has been spreading since May and has long since reached Europe. It traces back to an older viral lineage that has since largely disappeared from the infection landscape. However, the virus likely persisted in a person with a long-term infection and underwent significant changes through numerous mutations. Researchers from the Infection Biology Unit at the German Primate Center - Leibniz Institute for Primate Research, in collaboration with colleagues from Hannover Medical School, investigated how efficiently PJ.2.1 can penetrate human cells and how well antibodies from vaccinated individuals neutralize the new variant. The results show that PJ.2.1 binds more strongly than the other virus variants studied to the ACE2 receptor, which serves as the entry point for SARS-CoV-2 into human cells, and enters certain cells that produce only small amounts of ACE2 more effectively. Despite these changes, the new variant was effectively neutralized by antibodies produced following vaccination with the current booster vaccine, which has been adapted to the XFG variant. The results suggest that vaccination provides protection against PJ.2.1. However, this could change if the variant acquires additional mutations that enable it to evade the immune response (Journal of Infection, The Lancet Infectious Diseases). A hallmark of SARS-CoV-2 is the continuous emergence of new viral variants with changes in the spike protein, which allow the virus to partially evade the antibody response. Often, such variants differ from their predecessors by only a few mutations in the spike protein. These can alter binding sites for antibodies and/or influence binding to the ACE2 receptor, which the virus uses to enter human cells. In addition, however, variants may also emerge that are characterized by an unusually large number of mutations - particularly in the spike protein - and thus evade the existing antibody response particularly efficiently. Such so-called saltation variants can develop during long-term infections. In this process, the virus has the opportunity over an extended period to replicate within the body of an infected person and gradually undergo significant changes. Since May 2026, a new saltation variant of SARS-CoV-2 has been spreading: PJ.2.1. The variant was first detected in Canada and subsequently spread to the United States. Until now, it was unclear how efficiently PJ.2.1 can penetrate cells and how susceptible the variant is to neutralizing antibodies . In particular, it was not known how effectively antibodies produced following vaccination can inhibit PJ.2.1. A research team led by infection biologists Markus Hoffmann and Stefan Pöhlmann from the German Primate Center - Leibniz Institute for Primate Research, in collaboration with Georg Behrens's research group at Hannover Medical School, investigated these questions. Their findings show that PJ.2.1 is spreading rapidly in Canada, the U.S., and Spain; its prevalence is also rising in the Netherlands and France. A spread in Germany is therefore to be expected. With infection rates remaining high overall, the variant has been detected in all age groups. There is currently no evidence of more severe disease progression or new symptoms compared to other SARS-CoV-2 variants. The researchers found that the spike protein of PJ.2.1 binds more strongly to ACE2. Consistent with this, PJ.2.1 was better able than other variants to penetrate cells that produce only small amounts of the ACE2 receptor. PJ.2.1 was effectively inhibited by antibodies from individuals who had been vaccinated with the XFG-adapted mRNA vaccine Comirnaty, which is currently in use in Germany. In contrast, the SARS-CoV-2 variant BA.3.2, which is primarily detected in children, was only inadequately inhibited by these antibodies. Our results suggest that PJ.2.1 is likely spreading worldwide due to improved ACE2 binding. We assume that the XFG-adapted vaccine provides effective protection against PJ.2.1 as well as against the XFG viruses that are also circulating - at least as long as these viruses do not acquire mutations that allow them to evade the antibody response more effectively." Markus Hoffmann, German Primate Center - Leibniz Institute for Primate Research Stefan Pöhlmann adds: "Notably, neither the vaccine used last season nor the currently available vaccine elicits an antibody response that efficiently blocks BA.3.2 from entering cells. Since BA.3.2 is detected primarily in children, it should be investigated whether an additional component tailored to this variant could be included in future COVID-19 vaccines." Source: Journal reference: Happle, C., et al . (2026). Humoral immunity after mRNA SARS-CoV-2 XFG vaccination. The Lancet Infectious Diseases . DOI: 10.1016/s1473-3099(26)00569-4. https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(26)00569-4/fulltext

Temporal coverage within this national repository varied across the surveillance timeframe, with sequencing frequency reaching its highest peak in March 2023 with 343 analyzed genomes, followed by a secondary peak of 109 genomes in March 2024, reflecting operational realities where routine molecular testing ebbed and flowed alongside fluctuating clinical demand. Complementing the national GISAID sequence repository, the research team conducted an in-depth retrospective laboratory evaluation of 282 nasopharyngeal swab specimens confirmed positive for SARS-CoV-2 via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assays at the Aga Khan University Hospital Clinical Laboratories. Because the hospital operates a diagnostic network comprising more than 300 sample collection centers distributed throughout Pakistan, the laboratory cohort provided access to standardized clinical testing data and patient demographics that are frequently absent from international public sequence databases. Diagnostic screening was performed using the automated Roche Cobas 6800 system targeting the Orf1ab genetic region, and positive samples demonstrating cycle threshold values of 35 or lower were systematically charted to observe local testing trends. Of these confirmed diagnostic specimens, a subset of 223 samples satisfied the stringent quality criteria established for whole genome sequencing, which required a cycle threshold value of 26 or below to ensure sufficient template density for high-throughput multiplex library construction. The methodological workflow for clinical sequencing involved reverse transcribing viral ribonucleic acid into complementary DNA using specialized commercial synthesis kits, followed by dual-pool multiplex PCR amplification using validated ARTIC network version 3 primers designed specifically for SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery. Amplicons were converted into sequencing libraries using Illumina Nextera DNA Flex protocols and subsequently resolved on an Illumina MiSeq sequencing platform. Bioinformatic processing was carried out via the cloud-based CZID computational platform, which filtered out human host reads using minimap2 alignments against the human reference genome before aligning residual reads against the ancestral Wuhan-Hu-1 reference sequence NC_045512.2. Adaptor sequences were removed using Trim Galore, base calls were strictly retained only when sequence depth exceeded 10-fold coverage, and consensus variants were identified using samtools and BCFtools v1.20 to ensure analytical fidelity prior to downstream phylogenetic reconstruction. Phylogenetic lineage designations for the assembled genomes were systematically assigned using the Pangolin tool with the pangoLEARN algorithmic model, while Nextstrain clade classifications and amino acid substitutions were verified through Nextclade version 3.5.0. Multiple sequence alignments of complete viral genomes were generated using MAFFT version 7.505, after which maximum-likelihood phylogenetic trees were constructed utilizing IQ-TREE version 2.2.0 parameterized under the general time-reversible model with gamma-distributed rate heterogeneity across sites. Evolutionary rates and branch lengths were computed using the Augur bioinformatics pipeline and TreeTime within a time-resolved framework, where molecular clock outliers were filtered using a four-times interquartile range threshold. To assess site-specific amino acid variability, positional Shannon entropy across all ten open reading frames was calculated mathematically based on the relative frequencies of observed residues, with visual representations generated in Auspice, FigTree, and custom R scripts. For international comparisons, the authors assembled global datasets from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and India over the identical twenty-one-month surveillance window. Because raw submission counts in GISAID were heavily skewed—ranging from 286,135 sequences from the United States to 14,734 sequences from India—the authors executed a monthly down-sampling algorithm to standardize statistical comparisons. Specifically, custom Python routines selected up to 300 representative genomes per country-month, retaining all available sequences whenever monthly submissions fell below that threshold. This normalization strategy generated standardized comparison datasets consisting of 6,300 genomes each for the United States, the United Kingdom, and France, alongside 3,435 genomes for India. Combining these standardized international cohorts with 780 representative Pakistani genomes enabled the construction of a comprehensive, time-resolved maximum-likelihood tree spanning Nextstrain clades 21L through 24E, providing an empirical basis for comparing lineage turnover and evolutionary rates across disparate health systems. Analysis of national lineage dynamics in Pakistan revealed a clear temporal progression among 86 distinct identified variants, though only 13 achieved relative monthly frequencies exceeding 20 percent. During the first half of 2023, viral populations were heavily dominated by recombinant XBB lineages, particularly XBB.1.19.1 and XBB.1.9.1, which collectively accounted for 39 percent of characterized genomes in March 2023. By August 2023, these ancestral recombinants were replaced by emerging sub-lineages GW.5, GW.5.1, and persistent XBB.1.19.1 strains, before transitioning toward FL.1 and FY.5 by October 2023. The pivotal evolutionary transition occurred in late 2023 with the introduction of the BA.2.86-descended variant JN.1. Unlike Western comparison countries, where JN.1 was rapidly superseded by newer progeny such as KP.3.1.1 during the spring and summer of 2024, Pakistan experienced prolonged JN.1 dominance throughout the surveillance window, with JN.1 and its sub-lineage JN.1.18 representing 77 percent of sequenced isolates in March 2024 and remaining predominant through September 2024 despite sporadic detections of KP.2, LB.1, and LA.1. Demographic and epidemiological evaluations performed on 213 sequenced samples at the Aga Khan University Hospital revealed that the vast majority of analyzed specimens originated from Sindh province, with Karachi and Hyderabad accounting for 94.8 percent of cases, alongside sporadic submissions from Punjab, Islamabad Capital Territory, Gilgit-Baltistan, Baluchistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Patient age distributions indicated that adults aged 19 to 50 years comprised 54 percent of positive cases, older adults aged over 50 years represented 44 percent, and pediatric individuals aged 1 to 18 years accounted for 3 percent. Statistical evaluations revealed no significant linear trend in case numbers across the study period via chi-square testing, reflecting intermittent wave-like epidemic surges rather than continuous increases. Furthermore, categorical analysis of 21 lineages across patient characteristics demonstrated no statistically significant associations between specific SARS-CoV-2 lineages and patient gender via Fisher’s exact test, patient age categories via chi-square analysis, or inpatient versus outpatient clinical status. When assessing molecular clock kinetics, the estimated nucleotide substitution rate for SARS-CoV-2 in Pakistan was calculated at 4.67 times 10 to the negative fourth power substitutions per site per year, accompanied by a 95 percent confidence interval extending from 3.29 times 10 to the negative fourth power to 6.04 times 10 to the negative fourth power. This measured substitution rate was statistically indistinguishable from the rates calculated for Western nations, where point estimates ranged between 4.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power and 5.22 times 10 to the negative fourth power per site per year. Formal meta-analytic evaluation using Cochran’s Q test confirmed an absence of significant overall heterogeneity among substitution rates observed in Pakistan, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. In contrast, genomes analyzed from India exhibited a significantly lower estimated substitution rate of 6.92 times 10 to the negative fifth power per site per year, though this figure was accompanied by an unusually wide confidence interval ranging from zero to 1.4 times 10 to the negative fourth power, suggesting underlying data constraints or differences in lineage sampling rather than true biological divergence. Genomic diversity analyses revealed that SARS-CoV-2 isolates in Pakistan exhibited a mean positional Shannon entropy of 0.0324 across the complete coding sequence, a figure noticeably higher than the baseline positional entropy values recorded for the United States at 0.0100, the United Kingdom at 0.0107, France at 0.0105, and India at 0.0129. Across all examined geographical regions, mutational density was consistently concentrated within the spike glycoprotein gene region, followed by open reading frame 1ab and the membrane protein gene, aligning with known selective pressures directed against viral surface antigens. While the elevated genomic entropy observed in Pakistan mirrors findings from prolonged national surveillance in other settings where post-outbreak diversification accumulates, the study authors explicitly noted that this elevated metric could partially reflect sampling dynamics inherent to smaller, geographically concentrated datasets rather than purely elevated viral mutation rates in vivo. Interpretation of these epidemiological findings must be framed within several methodological and structural limitations acknowledged by the investigators. First, the total volume of genomic sequencing performed in Pakistan was modest compared to high-resource nations, driven by constrained diagnostic resources where national testing capacity peaked at approximately 46,500 tests daily during 2021 compared to 1 million daily tests in the United States. Second, because clinical severity metrics and vaccination histories were unavailable for the vast majority of sequenced isolates, the authors could not directly correlate specific lineage replacements with clinical outcomes or immune breakthrough frequencies. Third, geographic representation was heavily skewed toward Sindh province due to the centralized location of the sequencing infrastructure in Karachi, leaving rural provinces underrepresented. Despite these constraints, the study provides foundational documentation of post-pandemic viral evolution in Pakistan, illustrating how regional vaccine platforms—dominated by inactivated formulations such as Sinopharm and SinoVac—alongside distinct population demographics can foster localized evolutionary niches that sustain major viral lineages long after their global displacement. The case report, published in Laboratory Animal Research, documents a solitary round cell neoplasm within the brain of a 19-week-old male k18-hACE2 mouse that had been inoculated intranasally with the virus as part of an experimental investigation. Microscopic and molecular examinations revealed viral antigens localized directly inside tumor-associated histiocytes and adjacent cortical neurons, providing an initial documented observation of SARS-CoV-2 tropism within a primary central nervous system tumor in this animal model. Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 is recognized primarily as a respiratory pathogen causing coronavirus disease 2019, but neurological manifestations frequently accompany acute infection. Reported complications in humans include headache, anosmia, encephalitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, seizures, delirium, dementia-like syndromes, and psychiatric disorders, reflecting the neuroinvasive capability of the pathogen. Neurological signs and tissue lesions have been reported in 36.4 percent of human patients who succumbed to COVID-19. Cellular neuroinvasion is linked to the presence of human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors, which are widely expressed throughout the central nervous system across neurons, microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, in addition to epithelial linings of the respiratory and digestive tracts. To evaluate viral dynamics and neuropathology, researchers commonly utilize the k18-hACE2 transgenic mouse strain, in which human ACE2 expression is driven under the control of the cytokeratin 18 promoter. This transgenic lineage develops substantial viral neuroinvasion, severe encephalitis, and elevated mortality following viral exposure. While previous investigations have explored whether viral infections modulate cancer initiation or accelerate malignant progression, primary histiocytic and lymphoproliferative disorders of the central nervous system remain exceptionally rare in laboratory mice. Primary central nervous system lymphomas account for aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphomas, with diffuse large B-cell lymphomas representing 90 percent of human cases, often associated with immune dysfunction or oncogenic viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus and human immunodeficiency virus. Discover more Infection infection Check Symptoms infections Study Biology The affected male mouse was housed within biosafety level 3 facilities at the VISAVET health surveillance center and challenged intranasally with a viral suspension of 25 microliters containing 10,000 tissue culture infectious doses (50 percent end point). The animal was monitored daily for clinical progression, including changes in body weight, coat condition, activity levels, eye closure, and respiratory or neurological distress. By the seventh day post-infection, marked clinical deterioration was evident, characterized by pronounced inactivity, closed eyes, and a 10 percent loss in body weight, prompting humane euthanasia. Post-mortem examination and comprehensive necropsy were conducted immediately to recover organs for quantitative virological evaluation and full-body histopathology. Viral quantification was conducted on recovered tissues using a reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction assay with confirmed sensitivity down to 10 viral copies. The initial viral inoculum registered a concentration of 1.94 million copies per microliter. Within harvested animal tissues at seven days post-infection, viral burden reached 165,000 copies per microliter in brain tissue, compared to 120 copies per microliter in the lungs and 260 copies per microliter in the trachea and nasal turbinates. These measurements demonstrated significant viral replication and high tropism within the central nervous system compartment relative to the primary respiratory entry sites. Gross anatomical inspection revealed focal pulmonary congestion accompanied by dark reddish areas of consolidation in the cranial lung lobes, while other major visceral organs appeared grossly unremarkable. Histopathological examination of the respiratory tract identified bronchointerstitial pneumonia accompanied by epithelial hyperplasia of bronchioles and type II pneumocytes, with evidence of mild perivascular edema and focal vascular thrombosis. Histological analysis of non-neural peripheral organs confirmed the absence of metastatic lesions, indicating that the intracranial mass was a primary, solitary neoplasm originating within the central nervous system. Microscopic evaluation of brain sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin demonstrated an oval, well-demarcated leptomeningeal tumor positioned over the secondary somatosensory cortex within the diencephalic subdivision. The mass measured 1,340 micrometers in length by 590 micrometers in width and was completely enveloped by a thin fibroblastic capsule. The neoplastic mass exhibited moderate neovascularization and a mild to moderate presence of mitotic figures. Cellular composition comprised dense accumulations of mononuclear round cells resembling lymphoblasts with indented nuclei, intermixed with larger atypical lymphocytes and abundant, paler histiocytic cells featuring prominent nucleoli. Discover more infectious Find Cancer Care Try Brain Games Study Anatomy Find Neurologists The surrounding brain parenchyma presented acute histopathological changes characteristic of severe neuroinvasive viral infection. Sections exhibited diffuse meningoencephalitis, perivascular lymphocytic cuffing, widespread vasculitis, increased glial cell proliferation, and vacuolation along white matter myelin tracts. Cortical neurons displayed degenerative alterations, including cytoplasmic vacuolization and pyknotic, eccentrically displaced nuclei. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed extensive viral antigen expression across cortical layers IV and V, hippocampal pyramidal neurons, the stratum radiatum of the CA1 region, and local microglial extensions. Detailed immunohistochemical characterization of the neoplastic mass resolved phenotypic markers across distinct cell populations. The abundant histiocytic cells demonstrated intense cytoplasmic immunoreactivity for ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba-1), predominantly organized at the outer margins of the tumor. Conversely, the central mononuclear lymphocytic cells lacked expression of the B-cell lineage marker PAX5 and the T-cell marker CD3, while CD3-positive T lymphocytes were restricted to perivascular cuffs in the adjacent neuroparenchyma. Furthermore, the tumor cells showed negative or negligible labeling for interferon regulatory factor 4 (IRF-4), excluding plasma cell neoplasia such as plasmacytoma or multiple myeloma. The lack of PAX5 expression ruled out a conventional diagnosis of histiocyte-rich B-cell lymphoma and led the investigators to hypothesize that the lesion represented a lymphoma undergoing transdifferentiation into a histiocytic or dendritic cell neoplasm. PAX5 is essential for maintaining B-cell identity, and its downregulation permits lymphoid progenitors to differentiate along macrophage and histiocytic lineages, as observed in histiocytic sarcomas. SARS-CoV-2 viral antigens were detected within the cytoplasm of neoplastic histiocytes located near infected neurons, potentially mediated by non-ACE2 entry pathways such as CD169. Due to the rapid seven-day timeline between inoculation and necropsy, the authors concluded that direct viral oncogenesis was unlikely, suggesting the mass arose spontaneously or advanced under acute viral-induced inflammation. To ensure diagnostic precision across the immunohistochemical evaluations, the investigators implemented rigorous procedural controls. Tissue sections prepared from a healthy mouse spleen served as positive reference standards for PAX5, CD3, and Iba-1 reactivity, whereas splenic tissue obtained from a mouse inoculated with myeloma cells provided a verified positive control for IRF-4 labeling. For negative controls, primary antibodies were systematically replaced with tris-buffered saline. Beyond identifying the mass itself, microscopic examination of the diencephalic region identified subtle structural alterations in the surrounding brain architecture. The positioning of the encapsulated nodule corresponded to the abrupt margin of the surviving cortical layer, suggesting that localized tissue atrophy had produced a loss of the lateroventral cortex directly adjacent to the lesion. The detection of viral antigen inside neoplastic histiocytes underscores questions regarding atypical viral entry mechanisms. Although SARS-CoV-2 neuroinvasion is predominantly facilitated by ACE2 expression, the researchers noted that the pathogen can penetrate histiocytes through type I lectin receptors, specifically CD169, without relying on ACE2 binding. This observed cellular tropism parallels earlier laboratory studies involving malignant cell cultures, which demonstrated active SARS-CoV-2 internalization in glioblastoma, hepatoma, and brain-metastatic lung cancer cell lines. In those experimental environments, infected cancer cells have been hypothesized to act as operational viral reservoirs that might facilitate viral dissemination during metastatic spread while directly affecting tumor progression and host survival. The authors also reviewed systemic immunological and molecular pathways that could link viral infection to lymphoid transformation. An established immunological concept involves an imbalance between T helper 1 and T helper 2 lymphocytes, which skews the immune response toward antibody-dependent pathways and correlates with elevated COVID-19 mortality. Molecularly, SARS-CoV-2 infection can upregulate microRNA miR-155, disrupting cellular regulation and promoting ongoing inflammatory cytokine signaling that stimulates B-cell proliferation. Additionally, the virus shares functional characteristics with oncogenic viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus and hepatitis B virus, which disrupt cellular defenses by promoting degradation of the tumor suppressor protein p53. Documented reductions in p53 levels among both acute and long COVID-19 patients further indicate a possible mechanism for elevated carcinogenic vulnerability. Microenvironmental stresses triggered by severe inflammatory cascades represent another contributing avenue under evaluation. Cellular responses to damage-associated molecular patterns and pathogen-associated molecular patterns generate localized tissue hypoxia. This hypoxic microenvironment stimulates the synthesis of lysyl oxidase, an enzyme that facilitates the migration and tissue invasion of neoplastic cells. Furthermore, isolated clinical reports have identified occurrences of B-cell and T-cell lymphomas following COVID-19 vaccination, where persistent lymphoid activation and chronic inflammation were implicated in malignant transformation. Although these vaccine-associated events remain rare, the authors posited that natural viral infection might produce comparable or more pronounced immune stimulation capable of influencing lymphoid stability in vulnerable subjects. The researchers emphasized notable experimental limitations that constrain definitive causal conclusions from this single case. The small overall dimensions and incipient developmental stage of the tumor restricted the availability of serial tissue sections, which prevented a more exhaustive diagnostic panel of immunohistochemical markers. In addition, the k18-hACE2 model carries inherent limitations due to the transgenic overexpression of human ACE2 under the cytokeratin 18 promoter, which induces unusually severe neuropathology and an exaggerated neuroinflammatory response upon viral challenge. Given the brief seven-day experimental duration and the rapid proliferation rate characteristic of murine tissues, the investigators could not exclude the possibility that the neoplasm developed spontaneously or arose through unrelated physiological factors rather than viral induction. records.content: Abstract Post-severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19) interstitial lung disease (ILD) encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of pulmonary abnormalities, ranging from resolving inflammatory changes to persistent fibrosis. Although most post-infectious abnormalities stabilize or regress over time, a subset of patients develop progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). Distinguishing post-infectious sequelae from newly emerging or previously unrecognized PPF is a diagnostic challenge. We present two cases of PPF following severe COVID-19 pneumonia. The first patient, a 57-year-old man, developed persistent hypoxemic respiratory failure following COVID-19 infection in 2020. After several years of radiological stability, following a new-onset pneumonia, progressive restrictive lung disease developed, marked by fibrotic abnormalities on high-resolution computed tomography of the chest (HRCT). Despite corticosteroid and mycophenolate mofetil therapy, the patient continued to deteriorate, with the development of PPF. The second patient is a 64-year-old man who presented with predominantly ground-glass lung opacities and restrictive lung disease following severe COVID-19 pneumonia in 2021. Initial corticosteroid treatment resulted in substantial radiological improvement and subsequent stability. However, in 2025, new fibrotic changes, including subpleural honeycombing, emerged with significant physiological deterioration. In both patients, the diagnostic evaluation was limited by the absence of conclusive histopathological findings, but because of radiological and clinical progression, antifibrotic medication nintedanib was initiated, and the patients were referred for lung transplant evaluation. Our cases illustrate the heterogeneous and potentially progressive nature of pulmonary abnormalities following severe COVID-19 infection. PPF may develop several years after severe COVID-19 pneumonia, even with initial radiological improvement or prolonged stability. Because of the unpredictable course of the disease, the authors recommend continued evaluation with lung function testing and serial HRCT. For patients who progress despite medical therapy, early referral for lung transplant evaluation is advised. Introduction The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19) pandemic resulted in health emergencies for millions worldwide. While many have recovered, the chronic sequelae of the disease continue to impact patients' lives. This is probably most apparent in those who survived severe COVID-19 pneumonia but develop interstitial lung disease (ILD), which often results in chronic disability. Little is known about the origin of post-COVID-19 ILD, but preliminary research based on lung pathology [1] distinguishes four types of interstitial lung changes: diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), organizing pneumonia (OP), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). While these entities were initially recognized on lung pathology, they are now commonly used in the clinical description of the disease based on imaging [2]. DAD and OP usually represent inflammatory changes early in the course of the disease, and fibrosis associated with NSIP or UIP may form later. However, the temporal and etiological relationship of these entities remains unknown. Progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) is defined as clinical, physiological, and radiological progression of already established pulmonary fibrosis. Patients must meet at least two of three criteria in the past one year: 1) worsening respiratory symptoms; 2) a change in pulmonary function test (PFT) marked by more than 5% decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) absolute value and/or more than 10% reduction in diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) absolute value; 3) radiological progression in the extent or severity of bronchiectasis, formation of new ground-glass opacity (GGO) or reticulation, new or worsening honeycombing, or increase in lobar volume loss [3]. The purpose of this article is to present the diagnostic complexities of post-COVID-19 ILD and to provide a practical approach for these patients. Case Presentation Case 1 A 57-year-old gentleman with a medical history of multiple transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), previous cardiac surgery for atrial myxoma, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, and a 22-pack-year smoking history developed severe COVID-19 pneumonia in April 2020. The disease course is shown in Figure 1. His occupational history was notable for asbestos exposure from work as a plumber, and he reported keeping two dogs at home. Although invasive ventilatory support was not required during the acute infection, he developed persistent hypoxemia requiring long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT). Initial PFT in October 2023 demonstrated restrictive ventilatory impairment marked by low FVC, low forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), and severe reduction in DLCO. Post-hospitalization chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed mild and stable post-inflammatory reticulation in 2024. In March 2025, he developed pneumonia, which was treated with antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids as an outpatient. Following this episode, his preexisting hypoxemia worsened, and he was seen in our ILD clinic. HRCT of the chest demonstrated progressive lung disease with extensive fibrotic interstitial abnormalities without a particular pattern but primarily affecting the lower lobes. Neither traction bronchiectasis nor honeycombing was identified. A stable 9 mm pulmonary nodule was also present in the right upper lobe. Representative CT images are shown in Figure 2. Given the patient's medical, occupational, and exposure history, post-inflammatory lung fibrosis, asbestosis, GERD-associated microaspiration, primary lung cancer, systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease (SARD-ILD), and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (CHP) were initially considered for the differential diagnosis of ILD. The differential diagnosis of ILD for Case 1 is shown in Table 1. Laboratory evaluation revealed only a low-titer positive antinuclear antibody (ANA; 1:40), while the remainder of the immunological work-up was unremarkable, suggesting against the presence of SARD-ILD. Both erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were within the normal range. PFT demonstrated progressive, severe restrictive disease. During the six-minute walk test (6MWT), exercise capacity was impaired, and the patient was able to walk only 60 meters despite continuous supplemental oxygen. To evaluate the right upper lobe nodule and the ILD, endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS)-guided transbronchial needle aspiration, core biopsy, and transbronchial cryobiopsy were performed. Lung tissue was obtained from the right upper and left lower lobes, and the mediastinal lymph nodes were also sampled. Histopathological and cytological examinations revealed no evidence of malignancy, excluded histological changes associated with asbestos-related lung disease, aspiration, and CHP, but did not provide an alternative diagnosis of the origin of the ILD. The bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was neutrophil-predominant without infectious agents. Systemic corticosteroid therapy in combination with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) was initiated in December 2025. Despite immunosuppressive treatment and completion of a pulmonary rehabilitation program, the patient's clinical condition continued to deteriorate, and his PFT declined in March 2026. HRCT of the chest in April 2026 demonstrated further radiological progression with early honeycombing. In view of the progressive fibrotic phenotype, antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib was started in April 2026. Cardiovascular assessment with stress echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular function without evidence of clinically significant cardiac dysfunction contributing to his functional limitation. At the same time, optimization of glycemic control with semaglutide was associated with a 5 kg reduction in body weight. The patient met criteria for PPF because of a reduction in exercise tolerance marked by increasing LTOT, decline in FVC, and worsening pulmonary fibrosis with new honeycombing on imaging. Given the progressive nature of the pulmonary fibrosis and the increasing home oxygen need up to 6 L/min by June 2026, the patient was referred for lung transplant evaluation. Case 2 A 64-year-old never-smoker gentleman was evaluated in the ILD clinic. He had a complex medical history including Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosed in 1999, treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy; hypothyroidism diagnosed in 2003; and a traumatic right-sided hydrothorax in 2007. In 2019, he developed diverticular disease requiring colostomy. His postoperative course was complicated by peritonitis necessitating reoperation in 2020, an incisional hernia with mesh repair, and another surgical intervention because of mesh-associated infection in October 2021. In December 2021, the patient developed severe COVID-19 pneumonia. Following recovery from the acute infection, LTOT was prescribed because of recurrent episodes of hypoxemia. Follow-up chest HRCT demonstrated multifocal, upper-lobe-predominant GGOs without traction bronchiectasis, accompanied by subpleural architectural distortion, reticulation, and air trapping. PFT demonstrated a moderate restrictive ventilatory defect and a moderate reduction in DLCO. The disease course for Case 2 is shown in Figure 3. Because of concomitant small-airway disease, inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting β2-agonist (ICS/LABA) therapy was initiated. In March 2022, the patient additionally received prednisone at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg/day for one month, followed by gradual tapering. A subsequent chest HRCT in May 2022 showed substantial regression of the GGO, with only mild residual post-inflammatory scarring. After three years of disease stability, in April 2025, the patient underwent coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and synchronized electrical cardioversion for atrial fibrillation. Amiodarone was subsequently initiated for rhythm control. Following completion of cardiopulmonary rehabilitation, his cardiac function remained normal. However, there was a decline in lung function in May 2025. Amiodarone was stopped due to concerns for medication-induced ILD, but there was no evidence of radiological progression on repeat imaging. Initially, we considered amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity, chemotherapy-induced ILD, and radiation-induced lung injury for this patient, but because there was no temporal association between the exposures and ILD progression, these possibilities were excluded. The differential diagnosis for Case 2 is shown in Table 2. Immunological laboratory investigations were also initiated to rule out a developing SARD-ILD, but immune serologies were within the normal range. By August 2026, chest CT demonstrated newly developed, early subpleural honeycombing in multiple lobes. In view of the newly developed fibrotic changes, lung biopsy was offered to further evaluate the etiology of lung fibrosis. The patient declined the biopsy and preferred initiation of treatment. Following shared decision-making, antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib was started in August 2026. The patient met criteria for PPF because of the decline in FVC and DLCO, and worsening pulmonary fibrosis with new honeycombing was noted on HRCT. Referral was made for lung transplant evaluation. Representative CT images are shown in Figure 4. Discussion Post-COVID-19 ILD is currently a broad term that encompasses any interstitial abnormality following a COVID-19 infection. Based on the results of several population-based studies, the risk of developing ILD as a result of a COVID-19 infection increases by 3.6 to 11 times, although the accuracy of the data is based on diagnostic codes [4,5]. In the absence of additional test results (PFT, laboratory and histological findings), the accuracy of these data and the subtype of the resulting post-COVID-19 ILD cannot be determined. Currently, the most significant risk factor for fibrotic post-COVID-19 ILD is the severe disease course, especially the presence of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) [6], but age, male gender, and a history of smoking may contribute to the development of the disease [7]. During follow-up HRCT examinations, the presence of reticulations, traction bronchiectasis, and honeycombing may indicate the presence of fibrosis and, consequently, the development of ILD. While GGOs develop within a few weeks as a result of inflammatory processes and typically show regression over the course of months, fibrotic changes appear later and generally remain stagnant [8]. Respiratory symptoms and a decreased diffusion capacity are more likely to occur in conjunction with persistent pulmonary abnormalities [8]. The link between immunological diseases and post-COVID-19 conditions has been the focus of research for years. Based on the available data, COVID-19 infection may increase the risk of various autoimmune diseases [9,10]. However, the relationship between autoimmune diseases and post-COVID-19 ILD has yet to be fully elucidated. The reports on newly diagnosed cases of SARD-ILD following COVID-19 infection are purely observational. These case reports describe SARD-ILD following COVID-19 infection that was associated with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, myositis, or mixed connective tissue disease [11-14]. In the reviewed literature, lung biopsies were either not performed, or the biopsy did not contribute to the diagnosis, which makes it difficult to find an etiological relationship between COVID-19 infection and ILD. The International Multisociety Consensus Statement, published in 2025, provides recommendations for managing post-COVID-19 CT abnormalities based on the available scientific data [15]. According to the consensus, a thin-slice HRCT scan is recommended 3-6 months after a moderate-to-severe COVID-19 infection, and the frequency of follow-up could be determined based on the clinical picture in accordance with the "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA) principle [15]. In a prospective cohort study, Hernandez-Argudo et al. found that persistent lung radiographic abnormalities on HRCT one year after COVID-19 pneumonia increased the risk of persistent lung fibrosis [16]. In their study, NSIP and OP were the most common imaging findings, but DAD, which is a presentation of ongoing ARDS, was also frequent. However, UIP, which is associated with PPF, was not common [16]. In contrast, Konopka et al. reported that nine of 18 lung biopsies performed 2-12 months post COVID-19 infection showed UIP pattern fibrosis [1]. The discrepancies between the radiographic and pathological findings are most likely the result of differences in the timing of sampling and also the distribution of ILD, which is not homogeneous in the lung. To overcome some of these diagnostic challenges, current guidelines do not recommend lung biopsy in patients with a typical UIP as it will not change the therapeutic approach [3]. In cases without a typical UIP on imaging, a lung biopsy can be useful, but its availability is often limited by the patient’s poor functional status. Table 3 shows the common pathological and imaging findings in post-COVID-19 ILD. The treatment of PPF post-COVID-19 is also challenging. In the absence of clinical guidelines, the general approach follows the wisdom of non-COVID-19 ILD [17]. In primarily inflammatory disease, usually determined by more than 10% of GGO per lung surface on HRCT [3], we use immunosuppressive agents, including MMF, to prevent progression to fibrotic disease. In patients with primarily fibrotic disease with less than 10% of GGO on lung surface imaging, antifibrotic medication is preferred. Antifibrotic medications have been studied in progressive post-COVID-19 lung fibrosis, including pirfenidone and nintedanib, but these did not show any significant improvement in outcomes [18,19]. However, these studies were criticized for their broad inclusion criteria. In the case of patients with progressive NSIP, the current guideline provides only conditional recommendations for treatment [18] because the initial radiological findings do not necessarily correspond with disease progression. Identifying subgroups that show potential for progression may help to pinpoint target populations in which antifibrotics can improve clinical outcomes. While there are no guidelines on how to monitor patients with post-COVID-19 ILD, in our practice, we follow them similarly to those with non-COVID-19 ILD. PFT and 6MWT are performed every three to six months to monitor for stability, and a chest HRCT is recommended if lung function declines. We would like to emphasize that taking care of patients with ILD requires a multidisciplinary approach due to their multiple comorbidities. This usually includes primary care physicians, physical therapy, radiology, rheumatology, cardiology, and pulmonology. In cases with continued functional decline or a need for new home oxygen support despite medical therapy, early referral for lung transplant evaluation is recommended. Conclusions Post-COVID lung abnormalities mostly stabilize over time. However, in a small proportion of cases, progression and pulmonary fibrosis occur, accompanied by a decline in lung function and quality of life. Patients with progressive disease need close multidisciplinary monitoring. Our case series is limited by its purely descriptive nature, which does not allow broader interpretation. While we cannot draw long-term conclusions from our study, further investigations are needed to determine which subgroup of post-COVID-19 patients are at risk of progression and require early intervention. Researchers investigated how epidemiologically emerging viral strains interact with human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, tracing changes across antiviral, inflammatory, and antigen-presenting functions using high-dimensional immunophenotyping, secretome profiling, and functional assays. The investigation utilized a human peripheral blood mononuclear cell in vitro model to assess cellular reprogramming across multiple viral lineages. Investigators exposed primary immune cells to the ancestral D614G strain, alongside the Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Omicron BA.1, and recombinant Omicron XBB.1 variants, systematically comparing the immune signaling and cellular remodeling triggered by each lineage. Discover more Read Med Journals Get Health Tips Check Symptoms Single-cell multi-omic profiling following exposure to Omicron BA.1 revealed substantial remodeling across the innate immune compartment. The analysis identified a particularly marked dampening of monocyte differentiation and functional maturation, establishing circulating monocytes as primary targets for innate immune alteration following viral challenge. Discover more Study Anatomy Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Direct tracking of viral components confirmed that the virus preferentially accumulated within monocytes. By conducting viral RNA mapping and detecting double-stranded RNA-positive cells, the study authors observed localized accumulation of viral material that directly coincided with transcriptomic reprogramming inside the monocyte population. Analysis of cytokine and chemokine production indicated that the emergence of Omicron altered the inflammatory baseline compared to earlier lineages. Omicron exposure produced a more balanced inflammatory profile characterized by preserved antiviral type I interferon responses and moderated chemokine induction, pointing toward a regulated virus-host equilibrium. The study demonstrated that this shifted equilibrium was associated with reduced innate immune-mediated tissue damage in vitro. While earlier lineages triggered distinct inflammatory patterns, the moderation of chemokine induction under Omicron exposure indicated variant-specific calibration of early host immune responses. In contrast to BA.1, the post-Omicron recombinant subvariant XBB.1 robustly re-engaged host antiviral pathways. Cellular stimulation with XBB.1 induced high type I interferon release and uniquely promoted interleukin-12p70 production, highlighting divergence among closely related Omicron sublineages. The induction of interleukin-12p70 by XBB.1 drove the expansion of specific dendritic cell populations, including antiviral, mature PD-L1-positive CD80-positive plasmacytoid dendritic cells and BDCA3-positive conventional dendritic cells. These expanded dendritic cell subsets directly supported the priming of CD8-positive T cells. The authors concluded that circulating variants possess intrinsic differences that govern monocyte targeting, inflammation, and antigen presentation. These observations provide a detailed laboratory framework for evaluating how progressive viral mutations influence innate immune defense and subsequent cellular interactions in vitro. Developed from the monoclonal antibody ADG20, or adintrevimab, VYD222 exhibits substantially improved potency and breadth across an array of emerging viral lineages despite extensive mutations in the viral spike protein that inactivated earlier therapeutic antibodies. VYD222 previously received Emergency Use Authorization from the United States Food and Drug Administration for pre-exposure prophylaxis of COVID-19 in selected immunocompromised adult and adolescent populations. In laboratory evaluations, researchers confirmed that the antibody maintains potent neutralization across a broad panel of emergent variants, including the recently dominant XFG lineage. X-ray crystal structures of VYD222 bound to the receptor-binding domains of both prototype SARS-CoV-2 and the Omicron BA.5 variant reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying its activity. These structural complexes illustrate how VYD222 accommodates specific spike mutations that previously allowed viral variants to evade earlier authorized monoclonal antibodies. Discover more Study Biology Get Rapid Tests Order DNA Kits Track Biotech Find Lung Care Structural evaluations show that multiple engineered mutations separating VYD222 from its parental antibody ADG20 occur in the second shell outside direct paratope contact residues. Deep mutational scanning further demonstrates that viral escape from VYD222 is constrained by structural compatibility requirements and the virus’s necessity to maintain host receptor binding. These structural and functional findings elucidate the escape-resistant neutralization properties of VYD222 against clinically relevant SARS-CoV-2 variants. The authors note that the mechanistic insights offer guidance for assessing risk associated with emerging viral lineages. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 23, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Captive Wildlife in South Africa Faces Ongoing SARS-CoV-2 Reverse Zoonosis Risks by November 18, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Captive Wildlife in South Africa Faces Ongoing SARS-CoV-2 Reverse Zoonosis Risks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A multi-year One Health investigation conducted across four provinces in South Africa has revealed continued risks of reverse zoonotic SARS-CoV-2 transmission from humans to captive and free-ranging wildlife. Researchers monitoring susceptible animal populations between 2021 and 2025 confirmed active viral infections and serological evidence of exposure in multiple captive carnivore species. The study evaluated a cohort of 92 animals situated across Gauteng, Limpopo, Western Cape, and Mpumalanga Provinces. Animals were selected for investigation based on the presentation of clinical respiratory signs, unexplained mortality, or opportunistic sampling among species recognized as having high susceptibility to coronavirus infection. Investigators collected respiratory specimens to detect viral ribonucleic acid and obtained serum samples to evaluate immunoglobulin G antibody responses against SARS-CoV-2. In addition to testing for SARS-CoV-2, the team comprehensively screened respiratory samples for other potential infectious agents, including alternative coronaviruses, influenza A virus, and paramyxoviruses, ensuring that co-infections or secondary respiratory pathogens were thoroughly characterized. Molecular diagnostic testing using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA in four of the 92 tested animals, representing an overall detection rate of 4.3 percent. These confirmed cases comprised three lions sampled in Gauteng Province during 2021 and an exotic jaguar housed at a private zoological facility in Limpopo Province during 2023. Notably, the infected jaguar developed severe systemic and respiratory pathology that ultimately resulted in the animal’s death, highlighting the lethal vulnerability of certain exotic felids to coronavirus exposure in managed captive settings. Discover more Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Book a Safari Beyond molecular detection of active shedding, serological screening indicated that viral exposure was substantially more widespread across captive populations than identified by polymerase chain reaction alone. Serological tests performed on 45 animals identified SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulin G antibodies in six individuals, establishing a seropositivity rate of 13.3 percent. The seropositive animals included three lions, one lynx, one puma, and one mongoose. While the lynx and puma remained entirely asymptomatic and were housed at the same zoological facility as the three infected lions, the seropositive mongoose exhibited overt respiratory symptoms following close human contact at a wildlife reserve in Mpumalanga Province. To investigate the transmission chain and potential human sources of infection, the research team instituted contact tracing among facility personnel. Screening of zoo employees and veterinary staff who had potential contact with the affected animals identified one veterinary student who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 RNA via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. Partial genomic sequencing and phylogenetic analysis performed on viral RNA recovered from the fatal jaguar case classified the pathogen as Omicron sublineage BA.2. The researchers concluded that captive wildlife and free-ranging species in close proximity to human handlers or visitors face an enduring threat of reverse zoonosis post-pandemic. The fatal progression observed in the exotic jaguar emphasizes the critical need for continued vigilance at human-animal interfaces. The authors emphasize that sustained, integrated One Health genomic and serological surveillance remains indispensable for detecting novel viral spillovers, tracking lineage diversifications across host species, and mitigating transmission hazards among vulnerable wildlife populations.
